body.text: The Thermodynamics of Soluble Compound Extraction

Most coverage of The Science of Coffee Extraction misses the structural details that actually matter in food. When you look closely at real-world evidence, clear patterns emerge that separate durable results from short-term noise.

Roasted coffee beans are composed of approximately 70% insoluble cellulose structures and 30% water-soluble chemical compounds, including fruit acids, volatile aromatic esters, caffeine, and bitter melanoidins. When hot water contacts ground coffee, extraction proceeds in a non-linear chemical sequence: bright organic acids (malic, citric) dissolve almost instantaneously, followed by sweet sugars and Maillard reaction compounds, and finally heavy astringent chlorogenic acid degradation products.
Key Metrology and Extraction Parameters

items: Total Dissolved Solids (TDS): The mass fraction of dissolved coffee solids in the brewed liquid, measured precisely via optical refractometers calculating light refraction angles.
Extraction Yield (EY) Percentage: The percentage of the dry coffee grounds mass extracted into the cup (EY = TDS Brew Mass / Dose Mass), with the specialty ideal resting strictly between 18% and 22%.
Bimodal Grind Size Distributions: High-end burr grinders engineered to produce tight particle peaks while minimizing fines which cause channeling and bitter over-extraction.
Water Chemistry Stoichiometry: Balancing magnesium (Mg2+) and calcium (Ca2+) cation ratios to bind volatile flavor oxygen atoms while maintaining bicarbonate buffer capacity to preserve acidity.

body.text: Channeling Dynamics in High-Pressure Espresso

Under 9 bars of hydrostatic pump pressure, water aggressively seeks the path of least resistance through the compacted coffee puck. Microscopic fissures (channeling) cause localized over-extraction of bitter quinic acids alongside under-extraction of sweet sugars. Modern baristas deploy Weiss Distribution Technique (WDT) needle tools to achieve isotropic puck porosity.
